questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Length of a Leg Given a Right Triangle
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/multistep-13931219/assets/d6ac763e0d22c900ed29c43009d72c78.png)

Lucy has a small rectangular pool at home. The diagonal has a length of $x+2,$ one side of the rectangle has a length of $x,$ and the second side has a length of $a(x).$

Current part:

Find the expression for the length $a(x)$ in terms of $x.$

$a(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider the right triangle formed by two sides and a diagonal.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/multistep-13931219/assets/1c97f7121591003f503cfbce056e0709.png)

According to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2{)}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {a}^{2} & =(x+2{)}^{2}-{x}^{2} \\ a & =\sqrt{(x+2{)}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\ a & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4x+4-{x}^{2}} \\ a & =\sqrt{4x+4} \\ a & =\sqrt{4(x+1)} \\ a & =\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{x+1} \\ a & =2\sqrt{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze the given polynomial:

$$
p(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-3\,600
$$

The degree ($n=3$) is odd, and the leading coefficient (${a}_{3}=1$) is positive. Therefore, the polynomial has the following end behavior:

* $p(x)→-\infty $ as $x→-\infty .$

* $p(x)→\infty $ as $x→\infty .$

Only the graph $D$ satisfies these conditions.

Current part:

Determine which of $x=5$, $x=10,$ and $x=15$ is a root of $p(x),$ and use this information to write down a factor of $p(x)$ in the form $(x-r).$

{{field-1}}

is a factor of $p(x)$
questions.worked_solution:
The factor theorem states that $(x-r)$ is a factor of a polynomial $p(x)$ if and only if the root $x=r$ is also a root of $p(x).$

Here, we consider the numbers $5$, $10,$ and $15$ as possible roots. Let's check each of these values in turn.

* $x=5$ is not a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & =(5{)}^{3}+(5{)}^{2}-3\,600 \\ & =125+25-3\,600 \\ & =-3\,450 \\ & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

* $x=10$ is not a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10) & =(10{)}^{3}+(10{)}^{2}-3\,600 \\ & =1\,000+100-3\,600 \\ & =-2\,500 \\ & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

* $x=15$ is a root of $p(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(15) & =(15{)}^{3}+(15{)}^{2}-3\,600 \\ & =3\,375+225-3\,600 \\ & =3\,600-3\,600 \\ & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the factor theorem, $(x-15)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

The polynomial $p(x)$ can be factored as

$$
p(x)=(x-15)\cdot q(x)
$$

where $q(x)$ is a quadratic polynomial. Find $q(x).$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To factor $p(x),$ we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-15)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-15)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-15)$ using synthetic division:

| | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $15$ | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-3600$ |
| | $↓$ | $15$ | $240$ | $3600$ |
| | $1$ | $16$ | $240$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-3\,600}{x-15}=({x}^{2}+16x+240),
$$

which means that

$$
{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-3\,600=(x-15)({x}^{2}+16x+240).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+16x+240$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac={16}^{2}-4(1)(240)=-704<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2}+16x+240$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative.

Therefore, the full factorization of $p(x)$ over the real numbers is given by

$$
(x-15)({x}^{2}+16x+240).
$$

Current part:

The equation ${x}^{2}+16x+240=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q$, and solve the equation.

$p+q\,=$
{{field-1}}
$,\,x=-8\,\pm \,\text{i}$

questions.worked_solution:
We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+16x+240 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+16x & =-240\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+16x & =-240 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 8x+{8}^{2}-{8}^{2} & =-240 \\ (x+8{)}^{2}-64 & =-240 \\ (x+8{)}^{2} & =-176\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=8,q=-176,$ and $p+q=-168.$

Finally, we solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+8{)}^{2} & =-176 \\ x+8 & =\pm \sqrt{-176} \\ x+8 & =\pm \sqrt{-16\cdot 11} \\ x+8 & =\pm 4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i} \\ x & =-8\pm \text{i}\,4\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-8+4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i}$ and $x=-8-4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's pick the complex number $z=-8+4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i}.$

For a complex number $z=a+b\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.
$$

For the complex number $z=-8+4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i},$ we have $a=-8$ and $b=4\sqrt{11}.$ So, the magnitude is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}|-8+4\sqrt{11}\,\text{i}| & =\sqrt{(-8{)}^{2}+(4\sqrt{11}{)}^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{{8}^{2}+{4}^{2}\cdot 11} \\ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}\cdot {2}^{2}+{4}^{2}\cdot 11} \\ & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}\cdot (4+11)} \\ & =4\sqrt{15}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
